variants.question: Which of the following is a fundamental physical quantity?
Which of the following is a fundamental physical quantity?
Which of the following is a fundamental physical quantity?

pq_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Fundamental quantities are independently defined base quantities of the SI system (length, mass and time); every other quantity is derived from them through multiplication or division, without introducing a new base unit.
pq_l1_t1.realPurpose: Recognising fundamental quantities helps you see how complex measurements like speed or density are built from simpler, standardised measurements.

variants.question: What is the SI unit of Length?
variants.subject: Length

variants.question: What is the SI unit of Mass?
variants.subject: Mass

variants.question: What is the SI unit of Time?
variants.subject: Time

variants.question: What is the SI unit of Electric Current?
variants.subject: Electric Current

variants.question: What is the SI unit of Temperature?
variants.subject: Temperature

pq_l1_t2.wrongAnswerTemplate: {{wrongAnswer}} is the SI unit of {{wrongSubject}}, not {{correctSubject}}.
pq_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: The SI system fixes exactly one base unit per fundamental quantity worldwide, defined using precise physical constants so measurements agree everywhere on Earth.
pq_l1_t2.realPurpose: A single universal set of units lets scientists, engineers and manufacturers share data and build compatible components without conversion errors.

variants.question: Speed is a derived quantity formed by combining which two fundamental quantities?
Volume is a derived quantity formed by combining which fundamental quantity with itself three times?
Density is a derived quantity formed by combining which two quantities?
Area is a derived quantity formed by combining which fundamental quantity with itself twice?

pq_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Every derived quantity is built entirely from combinations of the fundamental quantities through multiplication or division, which is why its unit can always be expressed in terms of the base SI units.
pq_l1_t3.realPurpose: Seeing exactly which fundamental quantities combine to form a derived one makes it possible to check whether an equation's units are consistent, a technique called dimensional analysis.

variants.question: Which instrument is commonly used to measure small lengths (like the diameter of a marble) with a least count of about 0.01 cm?
Which instrument is commonly used to measure mass by balancing it against known weights?
Which instrument is commonly used to measure very small lengths (like the thickness of a sheet of paper) with a least count of about 0.001 cm?
Which simple instrument is commonly used to measure lengths up to about a metre, with a least count of 0.1 cm?

pq_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Different measuring instruments are designed with different least counts to suit the scale of what they measure, from a coarse metre scale for everyday lengths to a fine screw gauge for extremely small thicknesses.
pq_l1_t4.realPurpose: Choosing the right instrument for the size of the object being measured ensures the result is both practical to obtain and precise enough to be useful.

pq_l2_t1.questionTemplate: A block has a mass of {{mass}} g and a volume of {{volume}} cm³. What is its density?
pq_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Density is a derived quantity found by dividing mass by volume; it inherits the precision limits of both the mass and volume measurements used to calculate it.
pq_l2_t1.realPurpose: Calculating density lets scientists identify unknown materials, check the purity of substances, and predict whether an object will float or sink.

pq_l2_t2.questionTemplate: The length of a rectangular sheet is {{length}} cm and its breadth is {{breadth}} cm. What is its area?
pq_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Area is a two-dimensional derived quantity found by multiplying two length measurements, so its unit is automatically length squared (cm², m²) without a separate base unit.
pq_l2_t2.realPurpose: Accurately calculating area is essential for tasks like buying the right amount of flooring, paint or fabric, and for scaling designs in engineering.

pq_l2_t3.questionTemplate: A substance has a density of {{density}} g/cm³ and a volume of {{volume}} cm³. What is its mass? (Mass = Density × Volume)
pq_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging the density formula (Density = Mass ÷ Volume) shows that mass can be found directly by multiplying density by volume, since density describes exactly how much mass is packed into each unit of volume.
pq_l2_t3.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used whenever a known material's mass needs to be estimated from its volume, such as calculating how heavy a manufactured part will be before it's built.

pq_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A substance has a mass of {{mass}} g and a density of {{density}} g/cm³. What is its volume? (Volume = Mass ÷ Density)
pq_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging the density formula the other way shows that volume can be found by dividing mass by density, which works because a denser material packs the same mass into a smaller volume.
pq_l2_t4.realPurpose: This calculation is used to estimate how much space a known mass of material will occupy, such as figuring out what size container is needed to hold a given mass of liquid.

variants.question: A student uses a metre scale (least count = 0.1 cm) and records a length as {{bad}} cm. What is the most likely error in this reading?
A student uses vernier callipers (least count = 0.01 cm) and records a length as {{bad}} cm. What is the most likely error in this reading?
A student uses a screw gauge (least count = 0.001 cm) and records a length as {{bad}} cm. What is the most likely error in this reading?

pq_l3_t1.answer: The reading has more decimal places than the instrument's least count allows
distractorPool: The instrument was held too far from the object being measured
The object was measured more than once
The measurement units were converted incorrectly
pq_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Recording more digits than an instrument's least count allows creates false precision — the extra digits are meaningless because the instrument cannot physically resolve differences smaller than its least count.
pq_l3_t1.realPurpose: Understanding least count stops students and technicians from reporting misleadingly 'precise' data, which could cause costly errors in manufacturing or scientific conclusions.

variants.question: While reading the water level in a measuring cylinder, a student's eye is positioned above the meniscus instead of level with it. The reading obtained will most likely suffer from:
distractors: Zero error
Least count error
Calibration error
variants.technicalIntricacy: Parallax error occurs because the line of sight is not perpendicular to the scale, so the mark appears to align with a different graduation depending on the viewing angle.
variants.realPurpose: Avoiding parallax error by reading scales at eye level ensures laboratory measurements and everyday readings (like a car's fuel gauge) are accurate.

variants.question: A vernier calliper shows a reading of 0.02 cm even when its jaws are fully closed, but a student does not subtract this from further measurements. This introduces a:
distractors: Parallax error
Random error
Unit conversion error
variants.technicalIntricacy: Zero error is a constant offset caused by the instrument's scale not reading exactly zero at its reference position, and it must be added or subtracted from every subsequent reading.
variants.realPurpose: Correcting for zero error ensures every measurement made with an instrument is consistently accurate, which is critical in precision manufacturing.

variants.question: A student calculates density by dividing a mass of {{massKg}} kg directly by a volume of {{volumeCm3}} cm³, without converting either quantity first. What mistake is being made?
variants.answer: Mixing units (kilograms with cubic centimetres) produces a numerically meaningless density value; both quantities must first be converted into a consistent unit system (such as both in grams and cm³, or both in kilograms and m³) before dividing
distractors: The student's method is correct, since density can always be calculated by dividing any mass unit by any volume unit without conversion
The mistake is only that grams should have been used instead of kilograms, while the volume unit doesn't matter at all
Density calculations never require consistent units, since density itself has no units

pq_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Density = Mass ÷ Volume only produces a physically meaningful result when both quantities are expressed in a matched unit system, since dividing kilograms by cubic centimetres mixes a unit roughly a thousand times too large with one that is comparatively tiny, badly distorting the result.
pq_l3_t3.realPurpose: Careful unit conversion before calculation is one of the most important habits in physics, preventing errors that can be off by orders of magnitude.

variants.question: A student rounds every measurement to the nearest whole number before performing a calculation, even when the instrument's least count allows for one or two decimal places. What is the consequence of this habit?
variants.answer: Rounding too early discards real precision the instrument actually captured, and this lost precision can accumulate through multi-step calculations, producing a less accurate final result than the instrument's readings actually supported
distractors: The habit is harmless, since rounding at any stage of a calculation always produces the exact same final answer
Rounding early is actually more accurate, because it removes any risk of a calculator error later in the process
The habit only matters if the instrument's least count is smaller than 0.001 cm; otherwise early rounding is always fine

pq_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Each premature rounding step throws away part of the genuine precision an instrument provided; when several rounded values are then combined through multiplication or division, those small individual errors can combine and grow, sometimes shifting the final answer noticeably away from the true value.
pq_l3_t4.realPurpose: Keeping full precision until the very last step of a calculation (and rounding only the final answer) is standard scientific practice, precisely to avoid this kind of accumulated error.

variants.question: What is the standard SI unit of area?
Which unit is commonly used to measure the area of a small object, like a book page or a postage stamp?

pq_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Because area is built by multiplying two length measurements together, its unit is automatically a length unit squared, with the square metre chosen as the SI base unit for area.
pq_l1_t5.realPurpose: Knowing the correct unit for area prevents mixing up area with length or volume when reading technical drawings, land records or shopping receipts for flooring and fabric.

variants.question: Which formula is used to calculate the area of a rectangle?
Which formula is used to calculate the area of a square?

pq_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: A rectangle's area formula multiplies its two distinct side lengths, while a square's area formula simplifies to squaring a single side length, since all four of its sides are equal.
pq_l1_t6.realPurpose: These two formulas are the starting point for almost every practical area calculation, from sizing a rug to laying out a garden bed.

variants.question: Which instrument would be most suitable for measuring the length and breadth of a large tabletop, in order to calculate its area?
Which instrument would be most suitable for measuring the length and breadth of a small rectangular card, in order to calculate its area?

pq_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: The lengths needed for an area calculation should be measured with an instrument whose range and least count suit the size of the object, a flexible tape for large surfaces and a rigid scale for small, flat objects.
pq_l1_t7.realPurpose: Choosing the right length-measuring instrument before calculating an area avoids both impractical measurements and unnecessary loss of precision.

variants.question: Why is area always expressed in square units, such as cm² or m²?
variants.answer: Because area is calculated by multiplying two length measurements together
distractors: Because area can only be measured using square-shaped instruments
Because area is a fundamental quantity with its own base unit
Because square units simply make the resulting numbers look larger

pq_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying two quantities that are each measured in metres produces a result measured in metres times metres, written as metres squared, which is why every area unit carries an exponent of 2.
pq_l1_t8.realPurpose: Recognising why area units are squared helps students avoid careless errors when converting between area units or checking whether a calculated answer is dimensionally sensible.

variants.question: When converting an area measurement from square metres (m²) to square centimetres (cm²), what must be done to the linear conversion factor (1 m = 100 cm)?
variants.answer: It must be squared (100 × 100 = 10,000), since area involves two length dimensions
distractors: It can be used directly without any change
It must be divided by itself
It must be doubled instead of squared

pq_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Since area is formed by multiplying two lengths, converting an area between units requires applying the linear conversion factor twice (once for each length dimension), which is the same as squaring it.
pq_l1_t9.realPurpose: This squaring rule is essential whenever architects, surveyors or students need to convert land or floor areas between different unit systems without distorting the true size.

variants.question: A square is best described as a special type of rectangle in which...
variants.answer: All four sides are equal in length
distractors: Only the opposite sides are equal in length
It has no right angles
Its area is always smaller than that of a rectangle

pq_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: A rectangle only requires opposite sides to be equal and all angles to be right angles; a square meets both of these conditions and adds the extra requirement that every side be the same length.
pq_l1_t10.realPurpose: Understanding this relationship explains why the square's area formula (side²) is really just a simplified case of the rectangle's area formula (length × breadth).

variants.question: Which of these best describes 'perimeter', to distinguish it clearly from area?
variants.answer: The total distance measured around the outer boundary of a shape
distractors: The amount of two-dimensional surface enclosed within a shape's boundary
The three-dimensional space occupied by a shape
The mass of the material used to construct the shape

pq_l1_t11.technicalIntricacy: Perimeter is a one-dimensional length measurement found by adding up the sides of a shape, whereas area is a two-dimensional measurement found by multiplying lengths together, so the two describe entirely different properties of the same shape.
pq_l1_t11.realPurpose: Confusing perimeter with area is a very common mistake; keeping the two clearly separate matters whenever fencing (perimeter) and flooring (area) are being planned for the very same space.

variants.question: Which of these real-world tasks primarily requires calculating AREA, rather than volume or mass?
variants.answer: Deciding how many floor tiles are needed to cover a room
distractors: Deciding how much water a storage tank can hold
Deciding how heavy a delivery package is
Deciding how fast a vehicle is travelling

pq_l1_t12.technicalIntricacy: Tiling a floor is fundamentally about covering a two-dimensional surface completely, which is precisely what an area calculation measures, unlike volume (three-dimensional capacity) or mass (amount of matter).
pq_l1_t12.realPurpose: Recognising which physical quantity a real task actually depends on is the first step to choosing the correct formula, rather than guessing or misapplying one meant for a different quantity.

pq_l2_t5.questionTemplate: A square garden has a side length of {{side}} m. What is its area?
pq_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: A square's area is found by squaring its side length; a common mistake is to instead multiply the side by 4, which actually gives the square's perimeter, not its area.
pq_l2_t5.realPurpose: This calculation is used whenever the size of a square plot, tile, or panel needs to be found from a single measured side.

pq_l2_t6.questionTemplate: A rectangular plot has an area of {{areaM2}} m². What is this area in cm²? (1 m² = 10,000 cm²)
pq_l2_t6.technicalIntricacy: Converting m² to cm² requires multiplying by 10,000 (100 squared), not by 100, since area conversion factors must be squared to account for both length dimensions.
pq_l2_t6.realPurpose: This conversion is used whenever a large area measured in square metres needs to be expressed in the smaller square-centimetre units used for detailed technical drawings.

pq_l2_t7.questionTemplate: A rectangular wall has an area of {{area}} m² and a length of {{length}} m. What is its breadth? (Breadth = Area ÷ Length)
pq_l2_t7.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging the rectangle area formula shows that breadth can be found by dividing the area by the length, since the length and breadth together multiply to give exactly the area.
pq_l2_t7.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used whenever one side of a rectangular space is unknown but its total area and the other side have already been measured or specified.

pq_l2_t8.questionTemplate: A tabletop has an area of {{areaCm2}} cm². What is this area in m²? (1 cm² = 0.0001 m²)
pq_l2_t8.technicalIntricacy: Converting cm² to m² requires dividing by 10,000 (100 squared), since undoing an area conversion also requires the squared version of the linear conversion factor.
pq_l2_t8.realPurpose: This reverse conversion is used whenever a small, detailed area measured in square centimetres needs to be expressed using the larger square-metre units suited to full-scale plans.

variants.question: A student converts an area of {{areaM2}} m² to cm² by multiplying by 100 (the linear conversion factor) instead of 10,000. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: The student used the linear conversion factor instead of squaring it; since area involves two length dimensions, the conversion factor itself must also be squared (100 × 100 = 10,000) to correctly convert m² into cm²
distractors: The mistake is negligible, since 100 and 10,000 give results of roughly the same size
Area conversions never require squaring the conversion factor, unlike volume conversions
The student should have used 1000 instead of 100, since that is the conversion factor used for mass

pq_l3_t5.technicalIntricacy: Using an unsquared linear factor to convert an area under-multiplies the true value by a factor of 100, since every length dimension in the area needs its own copy of the conversion factor applied.
pq_l3_t5.realPurpose: This is one of the most common real-world unit-conversion mistakes, and catching it prevents wildly undersized area estimates in technical and construction work.

variants.question: Which of these correctly gives the formula used to calculate density?
Which of these correctly rearranges the density formula to find mass?

pq_l1_t13.technicalIntricacy: Density is defined strictly as mass divided by volume, and any correct rearrangement of that relationship (such as solving for mass) must preserve the same underlying ratio between the three quantities.
pq_l1_t13.realPurpose: Being able to recall and rearrange the density formula accurately is essential before attempting any numeric density, mass or volume calculation.

variants.question: Which of these correctly gives the formula used to calculate speed?
Which of these correctly rearranges the speed formula to find distance?

pq_l1_t14.technicalIntricacy: Speed is defined as distance covered divided by the time taken, and rearranging this relationship algebraically (for example, to solve for distance) must always keep the same three quantities linked in the same proportional way.
pq_l1_t14.realPurpose: Recalling the speed formula and its rearrangements accurately is the foundation for every subsequent calculation involving distance, time or speed.

variants.question: Which of the following is a correctly written unit for density?
Which of the following is a correctly written unit for density expressed in SI base units?

pq_l1_t15.technicalIntricacy: Because density is mass divided by volume, its unit is always a mass unit divided by a volume unit, such as grams per cubic centimetre or kilograms per cubic metre.
pq_l1_t15.realPurpose: Recognising valid density units helps catch obviously wrong answers immediately, before even checking the numerical value of a calculation.

variants.question: Which unit is the SI unit commonly used to express speed in physics calculations?
Which unit is most commonly used to express the speed of vehicles on roads?

pq_l1_t16.technicalIntricacy: Speed's unit is always a length unit divided by a time unit; physics calculations typically use metres per second, while everyday road travel is usually described in kilometres per hour.
pq_l1_t16.realPurpose: Recognising the correct unit for speed, and telling it apart from density's mass-over-volume units, prevents units from two entirely different quantities from being mixed up.

variants.question: An object will float in water if its overall density is...
variants.answer: Less than the density of water

variants.question: An object will sink in water if its overall density is...
variants.answer: Greater than the density of water

distractorPool: Less than the density of water
Greater than the density of water
Unrelated to whether it floats or sinks
pq_l1_t17.technicalIntricacy: Whether an object floats or sinks in a liquid depends on comparing the object's overall density to the density of that liquid, not on the object's mass or size alone.
pq_l1_t17.realPurpose: This density comparison explains everyday observations, from ice floating on water to a pebble sinking straight to the bottom of a pond.

variants.question: A large steel ship floats on water even though steel itself is denser than water. What explains this?
variants.answer: The ship's hollow shape spreads its mass over a much larger volume, giving it an overall (average) density lower than that of water
distractors: Steel actually becomes less dense than water as soon as it touches the surface
The ship's engines constantly push it upward to prevent it from sinking
Any sufficiently large object will float automatically, regardless of its material

pq_l1_t18.technicalIntricacy: A ship's hull encloses a large volume of air and empty space, so the ship's total mass divided by its total (hollow) volume gives an average density lower than solid steel's density, and lower than water's.
pq_l1_t18.realPurpose: This principle of average density, rather than material density alone, is exactly why massive steel ships can float while a solid steel block of the same mass would sink.

variants.question: Which instrument is used to directly measure the time taken by a moving object, a value needed to calculate its speed?
distractors: A beam balance
Vernier callipers
A screw gauge

pq_l1_t19.technicalIntricacy: Calculating speed requires both a distance measurement and a time measurement, and a stopwatch is the standard instrument for accurately timing how long a journey or motion takes.
pq_l1_t19.realPurpose: Pairing a stopwatch with a length-measuring instrument is the basic experimental setup used to measure speed in a classroom or sports timing context.

variants.question: Density and speed are both examples of which kind of physical quantity?
variants.answer: Derived quantities, since each is calculated by dividing one quantity by another
distractors: Fundamental quantities, since each can be measured directly with one instrument
Quantities that have no units at all
Quantities that can only ever be measured using a beam balance

pq_l1_t20.technicalIntricacy: Both density (mass ÷ volume) and speed (distance ÷ time) are formed entirely by dividing one measured quantity by another, which is the defining feature of a derived quantity.
pq_l1_t20.realPurpose: Recognising density and speed as derived quantities reinforces how every complex measurement in physics traces back to combinations of the same few fundamental quantities.

pq_l2_t9.questionTemplate: A train travels at a speed of {{speed}} km/h for {{time}} hours. What distance does it cover?
pq_l2_t9.technicalIntricacy: Distance is found by multiplying speed by time, since travelling at a constant speed covers an equal additional distance for every additional hour spent moving.
pq_l2_t9.realPurpose: This calculation underlies journey planning for trains, buses and any transport running at a broadly constant speed over a set number of hours.

pq_l2_t10.questionTemplate: An object has a mass of {{massKg}} kg and a volume of {{volumeM3}} m³. What is its density in kg/m³?
pq_l2_t10.technicalIntricacy: Density in kg/m³ is found the same way as density in g/cm³, by dividing mass by volume, provided both quantities are already expressed in a matching kilogram-and-cubic-metre unit system.
pq_l2_t10.realPurpose: Working with kg/m³ directly is common in engineering and construction, where masses and volumes are typically measured in kilograms and cubic metres rather than grams and cubic centimetres.

pq_l2_t11.questionTemplate: A car travels a distance of {{distance}} km at a speed of {{speed}} km/h. How long does the journey take? (Time = Distance ÷ Speed)
pq_l2_t11.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging the speed formula shows that time can be found by dividing distance by speed, since a faster speed means the same distance is covered in proportionally less time.
pq_l2_t11.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used constantly for estimating how long a journey will take, given an expected average speed and a known distance.

variants.question: A student compares two objects and claims that the one with the greater MASS must always be denser. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Density depends on both mass and volume; an object can have a larger mass but an even larger volume, giving it a lower density than a smaller, lighter object
distractors: The student is correct — density depends only on mass, and volume has no effect on it
Density only applies to liquids, so comparing the mass of solid objects is irrelevant
A greater mass always means a greater volume too, so the two are effectively the same comparison

pq_l3_t6.technicalIntricacy: Density is a ratio of mass to volume, so a heavier object is not necessarily denser; its volume could have grown by an even larger proportion, actually lowering its density below that of a smaller, lighter object.
pq_l3_t6.realPurpose: Avoiding this common mass-versus-density confusion is essential for correctly predicting whether objects will float or sink, and for correctly identifying materials by their density.

variants.question: What type of motion is exhibited by the blades of a rotating ceiling fan?
What type of motion is exhibited by a car moving along a straight highway?
What type of motion is exhibited by the Earth revolving around the Sun?
What type of motion is exhibited by a pendulum swinging to and fro?
What type of motion is exhibited by a ball bouncing up and down in place?

mo_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Motion is classified by the path an object's particles trace: a straight line (rectilinear), a curved closed path (circular), spinning about a fixed internal axis (rotatory), or repeating back-and-forth (oscillatory).
mo_l1_t1.realPurpose: Identifying the type of motion helps engineers choose the right mathematics and machinery — for example, wheels use rotatory motion while pistons use oscillatory motion.

variants.question: A runner completes exactly one full lap of a circular track with a circumference of {{circumference}} m and returns to the starting point. What is the runner's displacement?
distractors: {{circumference}} m
{{half}} m
{{double}} m

mo_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between the initial and final position; since the runner ends exactly where they started, the straight-line separation is zero, even though the distance travelled equals the full circumference.
mo_l1_t2.realPurpose: Distinguishing distance from displacement is essential in navigation and sports science, where the path taken and the net change in position can tell very different stories.

variants.question: What term describes the rate at which an object's velocity changes over time?
What term describes an object that is speeding up over time?
What term describes an object that is slowing down over time?
What term describes motion in which an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time?

mo_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Acceleration specifically measures how quickly velocity itself is changing, which is why speeding up, slowing down, and even changing direction at a constant speed can all technically count as forms of acceleration.
mo_l1_t3.realPurpose: Precise motion vocabulary lets scientists and engineers describe exactly how a vehicle, projectile or machine part is moving, which is essential for safety calculations like stopping distances.

variants.question: Is a car accelerating away from a stop light an example of uniform or non-uniform motion?
Is a car cruising at a constant, unchanging speed on a highway an example of uniform or non-uniform motion?
Is a ball rolling down a slope, speeding up as it goes, an example of uniform or non-uniform motion?
Is the second hand of an analogue clock moving steadily around the dial an example of uniform or non-uniform motion?

mo_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Uniform motion covers exactly equal distances in every equal time interval, meaning speed never changes; the moment speed varies at all between intervals, the motion becomes non-uniform.
mo_l1_t4.realPurpose: Recognising uniform versus non-uniform motion is the first step in choosing the right formulas and graphs to describe how something moves.

mo_l2_t1.questionTemplate: A cyclist covers a distance of {{distance}} m in {{time}} s. What is the cyclist's average speed?
mo_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Average speed is calculated as total distance divided by total time, and does not account for variations in speed at different moments during the journey.
mo_l2_t1.realPurpose: Average speed calculations are used to estimate travel times, set speed limits, and analyse the performance of vehicles and athletes.

mo_l2_t2.questionTemplate: An object moves at a constant speed of {{speed}} m/s for {{time}} s. What distance does it cover?
mo_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: For uniform motion, distance is found by multiplying speed by time, since equal distances are covered in every equal interval of time.
mo_l2_t2.realPurpose: This calculation is the basis for estimating journey lengths from speed and travel time, used in everything from trip planning to satellite tracking.

mo_l2_t3.questionTemplate: An object speeds up from {{initialSpeed}} m/s to {{finalSpeed}} m/s in {{time}} s. What is its acceleration? (Acceleration = Change in velocity ÷ Time)
mo_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Acceleration is calculated by finding the change in velocity (final velocity minus initial velocity) and dividing by the time taken for that change, giving the rate of change per second.
mo_l2_t3.realPurpose: Acceleration values like this are used to compare how quickly different vehicles can speed up, and are essential in designing safe braking and acceleration systems.

mo_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A car travels at a speed of {{speedMs}} m/s. What is this speed in km/h? (1 m/s = 3.6 km/h)
mo_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Converting between m/s and km/h uses the fixed factor 3.6, which comes directly from converting 1000 metres into kilometres and 3600 seconds into hours at the same time.
mo_l2_t4.realPurpose: This conversion is used constantly in everyday life, since road signs and speedometers use km/h (or mph) while most physics formulas use m/s.

variants.question: A car travels the first half of a journey at {{speed1}} km/h and the second half at {{speed2}} km/h. A student claims the average speed is exactly {{wrongAverage}} km/h by averaging the two values. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Average speed must be found using total distance divided by total time, not by simply averaging the two speeds
distractors: The speedometer of the car must have been faulty during the trip
Average speed can only be calculated for a single unchanging speed
The distances covered in each half must have been different

mo_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Simply averaging two speeds ignores that more time is spent travelling at the slower speed over the same distance, so the true average speed (total distance ÷ total time) is always slightly less than the arithmetic mean of the two speeds.
mo_l3_t1.realPurpose: Correct average speed calculations matter for accurately estimating fuel consumption, journey times, and traffic planning.

variants.question: A student calculates speed by dividing a distance of {{distanceKm}} km directly by a time of {{timeSec}} seconds, without converting either quantity. What mistake has the student made?
variants.answer: The distance and time were not converted to the same unit system before dividing
distractors: The measuring instrument used was not calibrated correctly
The object must have been accelerating rather than moving at constant speed
The distance was measured along the wrong path

mo_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: Speed must be calculated using consistent units (e.g. both in metres and seconds, or both in kilometres and hours); mixing kilometres with seconds produces a numerically meaningless result that is off by a large, inconsistent factor.
mo_l3_t2.realPurpose: Unit consistency is a foundational skill in physics — mismatched units are one of the most common sources of real-world calculation errors in engineering and science.

variants.question: A student says an object moving in a circle at constant speed has 'no acceleration,' since its speed never changes. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Acceleration depends on the change in VELOCITY (which includes direction), not just speed; even though speed stays constant in circular motion, the direction of motion is constantly changing, so the object IS accelerating
distractors: The student is correct — an object moving at constant speed can never be accelerating, regardless of its path
The object is only accelerating if it is also changing its speed, so constant-speed circular motion involves zero acceleration
Acceleration only applies to objects moving in a straight line, so circular motion is exempt from the concept entirely

mo_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Velocity includes both speed and direction; an object moving in a circle continuously changes its direction even while its speed stays fixed, so its velocity is constantly changing — and any change in velocity, by definition, means the object is accelerating (this specific case is called centripetal acceleration).
mo_l3_t3.realPurpose: Understanding that acceleration can come from a change in direction alone explains why passengers feel pushed outward on a curving road, even if the car's speedometer reading never changes.

variants.question: A student assumes a heavier object always falls faster than a lighter one when dropped from the same height, based on everyday experience with something like a feather and a rock. What is the more accurate physics explanation?
variants.answer: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass, because gravity accelerates everything equally; the everyday difference we observe between a feather and a rock is caused by air resistance affecting the lighter, less dense object more, not by gravity treating them differently
distractors: The student is correct — gravity always pulls harder on heavier objects, making them accelerate faster when falling
Lighter objects always fall faster than heavier ones, since they require less force to move
Falling speed depends only on an object's shape, and has nothing to do with either its mass or air resistance

mo_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Gravity gives every object the same acceleration regardless of its mass; a feather falls more slowly than a rock only because its large surface area relative to its mass makes air resistance a much bigger factor for it — famously demonstrated by dropping a feather and a hammer together in the airless environment of the Moon, where they land at exactly the same time.
mo_l3_t4.realPurpose: This distinction between gravity's effect and air resistance's effect is fundamental to understanding motion, from skydiving to spacecraft re-entry.

variants.question: An object is said to be at 'rest' when...
variants.answer: Its position does not change with respect to a reference point over time

variants.question: An object is said to be 'in motion' when...
variants.answer: Its position changes with respect to a reference point over time

distractorPool: Its position does not change with respect to a reference point over time
Its position changes with respect to a reference point over time
It is not affected by gravity
mo_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Rest and motion are both defined relative to a chosen reference point; an object counts as at rest only if its position stays fixed with respect to that reference over time, and in motion the moment it does not.
mo_l1_t5.realPurpose: This precise definition is what allows rest and motion to be described consistently, rather than relying on a vague everyday sense of 'not moving.'

variants.question: A passenger sitting still inside a moving train is AT REST relative to...
variants.answer: The train (and the other passengers inside it)

variants.question: That same passenger, sitting still inside the moving train, is IN MOTION relative to...
variants.answer: A person standing still on the ground outside

distractorPool: The train (and the other passengers inside it)
A person standing still on the ground outside
Nothing — a passenger is always in a state of absolute rest
mo_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Whether the same passenger is at rest or in motion depends entirely on which reference point is chosen — the train's interior, or the ground outside — showing that rest and motion are always relative, never absolute.
mo_l1_t6.realPurpose: This example demonstrates why physics always requires stating a reference point explicitly before describing something as being at rest or in motion.

variants.question: What is the key difference between rotatory motion and circular motion?
variants.answer: Rotatory motion is spinning about an axis that passes through the object itself, while circular motion is the movement of an entire object along a circular path around an external point
distractors: There is no real difference — the two terms describe exactly the same kind of motion
Rotatory motion only applies to liquids, while circular motion only applies to solids
Circular motion always involves a fixed internal axis, while rotatory motion never does

mo_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: In rotatory motion, every part of the object moves around an axis running through the object itself (like a spinning top), while in circular motion, the whole object travels along a circular path around a point outside itself (like a planet orbiting a star).
mo_l1_t7.realPurpose: Distinguishing rotatory from circular motion prevents a very common mix-up in early physics, and matters when designing machinery that specifically requires one type of motion over the other.

variants.question: What term describes any motion that repeats itself after a fixed, regular interval of time?

mo_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Periodic motion is defined purely by its repetition at fixed time intervals, regardless of the exact path taken, which is why oscillatory motion (like a swinging pendulum) and circular motion (like a spinning wheel) can both be periodic.
mo_l1_t8.realPurpose: Periodic motion is the basis for timekeeping devices such as pendulum clocks, since a consistent repeating interval can be used to measure equal units of time.

variants.question: What is the key difference between 'distance' and 'displacement'?
variants.answer: Distance is the total length of the path actually travelled, while displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between the start and end points
distractors: They are always exactly equal, for any type of motion
Distance is a vector quantity, while displacement is a scalar quantity
Displacement is always greater than distance, for any journey

mo_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: Distance tracks the full path length regardless of direction changes, while displacement only cares about the straight-line separation between where an object started and where it ended up, so displacement is always less than or equal to distance.
mo_l1_t9.realPurpose: This distinction matters whenever the actual path taken differs from a direct route, such as comparing a winding delivery route's distance to its net displacement from start to finish.

variants.question: A child walks 5 m to the east, then walks 5 m back to the west, returning to the exact starting point. What is the child's total displacement?
distractors: 5 m

mo_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Since the child ends up exactly where they started, the straight-line separation between the start and end points is zero, even though the total distance actually walked adds up to 10 m.
mo_l1_t10.realPurpose: This simple back-and-forth example makes the distance-versus-displacement distinction concrete, showing displacement can be zero even when real distance was covered.

variants.question: Which of the following is the best example of periodic (regularly repeating) motion?
variants.answer: The steady tick-tock swinging of a pendulum clock
distractors: A ball rolling down a hill and gradually coming to rest
A car accelerating away from a stop light
A stone thrown once and landing on the ground

mo_l1_t11.technicalIntricacy: A pendulum clock's swing repeats at a fixed, regular time interval indefinitely (while wound), which is exactly what defines periodic motion, unlike the other one-off or decaying examples listed.
mo_l1_t11.realPurpose: Recognising genuine periodic motion, as opposed to motion that merely happens once or gradually stops, is essential before using it to measure or keep track of time.

variants.question: Which of the following is the best example of rotatory motion (spinning about a fixed internal axis)?
variants.answer: A spinning top rotating in place
distractors: A car driving down a straight road
The Earth revolving around the Sun once a year
A pendulum swinging side to side

mo_l1_t12.technicalIntricacy: A spinning top rotates about an axis running through its own centre, with every part of it moving around that internal axis, which is the defining feature of rotatory motion, unlike the Earth's yearly orbit around an external point (the Sun).
mo_l1_t12.realPurpose: Correctly identifying rotatory motion is essential for understanding how machines like wheels, fans and turbines are designed to spin about a fixed axis.

mo_l2_t5.questionTemplate: An object travels {{distance}} m at a constant speed of {{speed}} m/s. How much time does it take? (Time = Distance ÷ Speed)
mo_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging the speed formula shows that time can be found by dividing distance by speed, since covering the same distance at a higher speed always takes proportionally less time.
mo_l2_t5.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used to estimate how long a trip at constant speed will take, given only the distance and the expected speed.

mo_l2_t6.questionTemplate: A cyclist rides {{east}} m to the east, then rides {{west}} m back to the west. What is the cyclist's net displacement, taking east as the positive direction?
mo_l2_t6.technicalIntricacy: Net displacement is found by subtracting the backward distance from the forward distance (since they point in opposite directions), not by adding them together as if they were both in the same direction.
mo_l2_t6.realPurpose: This calculation shows why displacement accounts for direction, giving a smaller net result than the total distance covered whenever a journey doubles back on itself.

mo_l2_t7.questionTemplate: A car travels {{outDistance}} km away from home, then returns home along the very same route. What is the TOTAL DISTANCE travelled for the whole round trip?
mo_l2_t7.technicalIntricacy: Total distance is a scalar that simply adds up every metre actually covered, so a round trip's distance is double the one-way distance, even though the trip's net displacement back home is zero.
mo_l2_t7.realPurpose: This distinction is essential for tasks like estimating total fuel used on a round trip, which depends on distance travelled rather than on net displacement.

variants.question: A student says a tree is always 'at rest' since it never moves on its own. Considering the concept of frame of reference, what is the more accurate view?
variants.answer: Whether the tree is at rest or in motion depends entirely on the reference point chosen — it is at rest relative to the ground, but in motion relative to an observer inside a moving car (or relative to the Sun, since the Earth itself is moving and rotating)
distractors: The student is correct — objects like trees are always in an absolute state of rest, regardless of who is observing them
Only living things can be classified as being in motion or at rest; objects like trees are exempt from this classification
Whether something is at rest or in motion depends only on whether it can move under its own power, not on any reference point

mo_l3_t5.technicalIntricacy: Rest and motion are never absolute properties of an object; they only make sense once a reference point is fixed, and the same tree can correctly be described as both at rest and in motion depending entirely on which reference point is chosen.
mo_l3_t5.realPurpose: This relativity of rest and motion is a foundational physics idea, explaining, for instance, why everything on Earth's surface is technically in motion relative to the Sun despite feeling perfectly still.

variants.question: Which of these is a scalar quantity, having only magnitude and no direction?
Which of these is a vector quantity, having both magnitude and direction?

mo_l1_t13.technicalIntricacy: Speed only describes how fast an object is moving (a single magnitude), while velocity describes both how fast and in exactly which direction, making velocity a vector and speed a scalar.
mo_l1_t13.realPurpose: Keeping speed and velocity conceptually separate is essential once direction starts to matter, such as when combining or comparing motions in different directions.

variants.question: Two cars both travel at the same speed of 60 km/h, but one travels north while the other travels south. What can be said about their velocities?
variants.answer: Their velocities are different, since velocity depends on direction as well as speed
distractors: Their velocities are identical, since both cars have the same speed
Neither car has a velocity, since velocity only applies to accelerating objects
Velocity cannot be defined unless the cars are travelling in a circle

mo_l1_t14.technicalIntricacy: Even though both cars share the exact same speed of 60 km/h, their velocities differ because velocity includes direction, and north is not the same direction as south.
mo_l1_t14.realPurpose: This example makes clear why speed alone is not enough to fully describe motion whenever the direction of travel matters, such as in navigation or collision analysis.

variants.question: What is the difference between 'uniform velocity' and 'uniform speed'?
variants.answer: Uniform velocity requires both constant speed AND constant direction, while uniform speed only requires the magnitude of motion to stay constant
distractors: There is no difference — the two terms always mean exactly the same thing
Uniform velocity only applies to circular motion
Uniform speed requires a constant direction, while uniform velocity does not

mo_l1_t15.technicalIntricacy: An object moving at a constant speed but continuously changing direction (like in circular motion) has uniform speed but NOT uniform velocity, since velocity is only 'uniform' when neither its magnitude nor its direction changes.
mo_l1_t15.realPurpose: This distinction explains why circular motion at constant speed is still considered accelerated motion in physics, since velocity itself is not staying uniform.

variants.question: Since acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity, in which ways can an object's acceleration arise?
variants.answer: From a change in speed, a change in direction, or both together
distractors: Only from a change in speed, never from a change in direction
Only from a change in direction, never from a change in speed
From a change in mass, since acceleration depends on how heavy an object is

mo_l1_t16.technicalIntricacy: Because velocity has both a magnitude (speed) and a direction, any change in either one, or in both together, counts as a change in velocity, and therefore as acceleration.
mo_l1_t16.realPurpose: This broader view of acceleration explains why objects turning a corner at constant speed, and objects speeding up or slowing down in a straight line, are both correctly described as accelerating.

variants.question: Which of the following best distinguishes uniform motion from non-uniform motion on a speed-versus-time graph?
variants.answer: Uniform motion produces a flat, horizontal line, while non-uniform motion produces a line that rises, falls, or curves
distractors: Uniform motion always produces a straight diagonal line, while non-uniform motion produces a flat line
Both uniform and non-uniform motion always produce the exact same horizontal line
Non-uniform motion cannot be represented on a speed-time graph at all

mo_l1_t17.technicalIntricacy: A flat horizontal line on a speed-time graph shows speed staying exactly constant over time, which is uniform motion, while any change in the line's height over time shows speed varying, which is non-uniform motion.
mo_l1_t17.realPurpose: Reading motion graphs this way lets scientists and engineers quickly tell whether an object moved steadily or erratically, without needing to inspect every individual timestamp.

variants.question: A speedometer in a car directly displays which physical quantity?
variants.answer: Speed (not velocity, since it gives no information about direction)
distractors: Velocity, including the car's exact direction of travel
Acceleration
Displacement

mo_l1_t18.technicalIntricacy: A speedometer shows only a single numerical magnitude and never indicates which way the car is heading, which is exactly the definition of speed rather than the direction-aware quantity velocity.
mo_l1_t18.realPurpose: Recognising this limitation of a speedometer explains why a compass or GPS device, not the speedometer, is needed to know a car's direction of travel.

variants.question: If a car's velocity changes from moving north to moving east while its numerical speed stays exactly the same, has the car accelerated?
variants.answer: Yes — velocity has changed (its direction changed, even though speed stayed the same), and any change in velocity means acceleration has occurred
distractors: No, because acceleration only occurs when an object's speed itself changes
No, because a change in direction alone can never be measured or counted as acceleration
Yes, but only because the car's mass must have also changed

mo_l1_t19.technicalIntricacy: Velocity is a vector combining speed and direction, so changing direction alone, even while speed stays fixed, still counts as a change in velocity, and therefore as acceleration.
mo_l1_t19.realPurpose: This example reinforces that steering around a corner, not just speeding up or braking, is physically a form of acceleration.

variants.question: In one-dimensional motion, what does a 'negative velocity' typically represent?
variants.answer: Motion in the direction opposite to whichever direction was chosen as positive
distractors: Motion that is somehow slower than zero speed, which is physically impossible
A measurement error, since velocity can never be written as a negative number
Motion in which the object must be decelerating, regardless of its direction

mo_l1_t20.technicalIntricacy: Once a direction is chosen as positive for a one-dimensional problem, any motion in the opposite direction is represented with a negative velocity value, purely as a sign convention rather than an impossible or erroneous speed.
mo_l1_t20.realPurpose: Understanding negative velocity as a direction convention (not an error) is essential for correctly interpreting motion graphs and equations that use signed values.

mo_l2_t8.questionTemplate: An object starts with a speed of {{initialSpeed}} m/s and accelerates at {{acceleration}} m/s² for {{time}} s. What is its final speed? (Final speed = Initial speed + Acceleration × Time)
mo_l2_t8.technicalIntricacy: Final speed is found by adding the initial speed to the total change in speed (acceleration multiplied by time); leaving out the initial speed entirely is a common mistake that this problem's alternate answer represents.
mo_l2_t8.realPurpose: This calculation is the basis for predicting how fast a vehicle will be moving after a known period of steady acceleration, which is essential for safety and performance analysis.

mo_l2_t9.questionTemplate: A car travels at a speed of {{speedKmh}} km/h. What is this speed in m/s? (1 km/h = 5/18 m/s)
mo_l2_t9.technicalIntricacy: Converting km/h to m/s uses the factor 5/18, the exact reverse of the 3.6 factor used to convert m/s to km/h; multiplying by 3.6 instead of 5/18 is the mistake represented by this problem's alternate answer.
mo_l2_t9.realPurpose: This reverse conversion is needed whenever a speed given in everyday km/h must be plugged into a physics formula that expects m/s, such as a kinetic energy calculation.

mo_l2_t10.questionTemplate: A car travels at {{speed1}} km/h for the first half of a journey's TIME, and at {{speed2}} km/h for the second half of the journey's time (equal time spent at each speed). What is the car's average speed for the whole journey?
mo_l2_t10.technicalIntricacy: When a journey is split into two EQUAL TIME segments at different speeds, the simple arithmetic average of the two speeds correctly gives the true average speed, unlike the equal-distance case where simple averaging is inaccurate.
mo_l2_t10.realPurpose: Recognising when simple averaging of speeds is valid (equal time) versus invalid (equal distance) prevents a very common calculation error in average speed problems.

variants.question: A ball thrown straight up is caught again at the exact point from which it was released. A student says the ball's average velocity for the whole trip equals its average speed, since it 'covered the same distance' going up and coming down. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Average velocity equals displacement ÷ time; since the ball returns to its starting point, its net displacement is zero, making its average velocity zero — even though its average speed (total distance ÷ time) is not zero
distractors: The student is correct, since average velocity and average speed are always identical for any journey
Average velocity cannot be calculated at all for objects that move vertically, only for horizontal motion
The average speed must also be zero, since the ball returns to exactly where it started

mo_l3_t6.technicalIntricacy: Average velocity depends on net displacement, which is zero for any trip that returns to its starting point, while average speed depends on total distance travelled, which is never zero as long as the object actually moved.
mo_l3_t6.realPurpose: This distinction is essential for correctly analysing any round-trip or back-and-forth motion, from a thrown ball to a pendulum, where speed and velocity tell very different stories.

variants.question: What is the SI unit used to measure weight?
distractors: Kilogram (kg)
Gram (g)
Metre (m)

wt_l1_new1.technicalIntricacy: Weight is a force — the pull of gravity on an object's mass — so it is measured in the SI unit of force, the newton, not in kilograms or grams.
wt_l1_new1.realPurpose: Using the correct unit keeps weight (a force) clearly distinct from mass (an amount of matter), preventing the two from being confused in calculations.

variants.question: Which of these best distinguishes mass from weight?
variants.answer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays constant everywhere; weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass and can change from place to place
distractors: Mass and weight are just two different names for exactly the same physical quantity
Mass is measured in newtons, while weight is measured in kilograms
Weight is a fixed property of an object, while mass changes depending on location

wt_l1_new2.technicalIntricacy: Mass measures how much matter an object contains and is unaffected by location, while weight measures the gravitational force pulling on that mass, which depends on the local strength of gravity.
wt_l1_new2.realPurpose: This distinction explains why an astronaut's mass never changes, even though their weight is dramatically different on the Earth, the Moon, or in orbit.

variants.question: Which instrument directly measures the weight of an object as a force?
distractors: A beam balance
A metre scale
A measuring cylinder

wt_l1_new3.technicalIntricacy: A spring balance measures weight directly, by the stretch of a spring under the pull of gravity, while a beam balance instead compares mass against known reference masses and is unaffected by changes in gravity.
wt_l1_new3.realPurpose: This is why a beam balance gives the same reading anywhere, while a spring balance reading would change if used on the Moon, since gravity itself is different there.

wt_l2_new1.questionTemplate: An object has a mass of {{m}} kg. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as g = 10 m/s², what is its weight?
wt_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: Weight is calculated as Weight = Mass × g, so simply restating the mass value in newtons (without multiplying by g) is a common but incorrect shortcut.
wt_l2_new1.realPurpose: This formula is what lets an object's mass, measured once on a beam balance, be converted into its weight at any known local gravity, such as on the Moon or another planet.

variants.question: An astronaut has the same mass on the Moon as on Earth, but weighs about one-sixth as much on the Moon. What explains this?
variants.answer: Weight depends on the local strength of gravity, and the Moon's gravity is about one-sixth as strong as Earth's, while mass (the amount of matter in the astronaut's body) does not change with location
distractors: The astronaut actually loses matter from their body during the journey to the Moon
Mass and weight both change together in direct proportion, so this observation is impossible
The Moon's weaker gravity only affects objects made of metal, like a spacecraft, not a human body

wt_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: Because Weight = Mass × g, and the astronaut's mass is unchanged, the entire drop in weight on the Moon comes from the Moon's smaller value of g, not from any change in the astronaut's body.
wt_l3_new1.realPurpose: This real example is the clearest everyday proof that mass and weight are genuinely different quantities, not just two names for the same thing.

variants.question: In an electric bulb, energy is transformed from:
variants.answer: Electrical energy to Light and Heat energy

variants.question: In a burning candle, energy is transformed from:
variants.answer: Chemical energy to Light and Heat energy

variants.question: In an electric fan, energy is transformed from:
In a solar cell, energy is transformed from:
In a stretched bow releasing an arrow, energy is transformed from:

distractorPool: Electrical energy to Light and Heat energy
Chemical energy to Light and Heat energy
en_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Every energy-using device converts one form of energy into another useful (and often some wasted) form; identifying the input and output forms is the basis of studying energy efficiency.
en_l1_t1.realPurpose: Understanding energy transformations helps engineers design more efficient devices that waste less energy as unwanted heat.

variants.question: What type of energy is possessed by a stretched rubber band?
What type of energy is possessed by water stored at height in a dam?
What type of energy is possessed by a coconut about to fall from a tree?
What type of energy is possessed by a car moving on a straight road?
What type of energy is possessed by a bullet fired from a gun?
What type of energy is possessed by a wound-up toy spring?

en_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Kinetic energy depends on an object's motion, while potential energy depends on an object's position, state of strain, or configuration relative to a reference point.
en_l1_t2.realPurpose: Distinguishing kinetic from potential energy helps explain everyday phenomena, from why a raised hammer can drive a nail to why a moving vehicle needs brakes.

variants.question: Is Solar energy (from sunlight) classified as a renewable or non-renewable energy source?
Is Wind energy classified as a renewable or non-renewable energy source?
Is Coal classified as a renewable or non-renewable energy source?
Is Petroleum (crude oil) classified as a renewable or non-renewable energy source?
Is Hydroelectric energy (from flowing water) classified as a renewable or non-renewable energy source?

distractorPool: A form of chemical energy only, unrelated to renewability
An energy source that has already been fully exhausted worldwide
en_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Renewable energy sources are naturally replenished on a human timescale (like sunlight or wind), while non-renewable sources, such as fossil fuels, formed over millions of years and are being used up far faster than they can be replaced.
en_l1_t3.realPurpose: This distinction is central to modern energy policy and technology, as the world increasingly shifts toward renewable sources to reduce reliance on limited fossil fuel reserves.

variants.question: According to the Law of Conservation of Energy, what happens to the total energy in an isolated system over time?
variants.answer: It stays exactly the same, only changing form
distractors: It gradually decreases until it reaches zero
It gradually increases without any outside input
It fluctuates randomly with no consistent pattern

variants.question: When a swinging pendulum gradually loses height due to friction, where does the 'lost' mechanical energy actually go?
variants.answer: It converts into heat and sound energy due to friction and air resistance
distractors: It is destroyed completely and no longer exists anywhere
It transforms directly into additional mass for the pendulum
It disappears until the pendulum is pushed again, then reappears

en_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: The Law of Conservation of Energy is one of the most fundamental principles in all of physics: energy is never created or destroyed in an isolated system, only converted between forms such as kinetic, potential, heat and sound energy.
en_l1_t4.realPurpose: This law underlies every energy calculation in science and engineering, from designing efficient engines to understanding why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

en_l2_t1.questionTemplate: A body of mass {{mass}} kg moves with a velocity of {{velocity}} m/s. What is its kinetic energy? (KE = ½ × mass × velocity²)
en_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Kinetic energy grows with the square of velocity, not directly with velocity, so doubling an object's speed quadruples its kinetic energy.
en_l2_t1.realPurpose: Because kinetic energy scales with velocity squared, small increases in vehicle speed cause disproportionately larger stopping distances and collision forces — a key reason for speed limits.

en_l2_t2.questionTemplate: A body of mass {{mass}} kg is raised to a height of {{height}} m above the ground. What is its potential energy? (Take g = 10 m/s², PE = mass × g × height)
en_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Gravitational potential energy depends on the object's mass, the height above a chosen reference level, and the local gravitational field strength — change any one of these and the stored energy changes proportionally.
en_l2_t2.realPurpose: Calculating potential energy is essential in designing dams, roller coasters, and any system that stores energy by lifting mass against gravity.

variants.question: A ball is thrown straight up and reaches a maximum height of {{height}} m before falling back down. A student claims that at the highest point, all of the ball's energy is kinetic energy. What is wrong with this claim?
variants.answer: At the highest point the ball is momentarily at rest, so its energy is entirely potential, not kinetic
distractors: At the highest point the ball has maximum kinetic energy because it has travelled the farthest
The ball loses all of its energy at the highest point due to air resistance
Energy at the highest point cannot be determined without knowing the ball's exact mass

en_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: At the highest point of its path, the ball's velocity momentarily becomes zero, so its kinetic energy (½mv²) is also zero, while its potential energy (mgh) is at its maximum for that throw.
en_l3_t1.realPurpose: Recognising this energy transition is key to understanding projectile motion, pendulums, and any system that continually converts energy between kinetic and potential forms.

variants.question: A student observes a swinging pendulum gradually losing height/swing over time and says energy has 'disappeared'. According to the Law of Conservation of Energy, what has actually happened to the missing energy?
variants.answer: The energy is not lost — it is converted into heat and sound by friction and air resistance
distractors: The energy has been completely destroyed and no longer exists anywhere
The energy has converted entirely into additional mass of the object
The measuring equipment must have made an error in tracking the energy

variants.question: A student observes a bouncing rubber ball gradually losing height/swing over time and says energy has 'disappeared'. According to the Law of Conservation of Energy, what has actually happened to the missing energy?
variants.answer: The energy is not lost — it is converted into heat and sound by friction and air resistance
distractors: The energy has been completely destroyed and no longer exists anywhere
The energy has converted entirely into additional mass of the object
The measuring equipment must have made an error in tracking the energy

variants.question: A student observes a ball rolling along a rough floor gradually slowing down over time and says energy has 'disappeared'. According to the Law of Conservation of Energy, what has actually happened to the missing energy?
variants.answer: The energy is not lost — it is converted into heat and sound by friction and air resistance
distractors: The energy has been completely destroyed and no longer exists anywhere
The energy has converted entirely into additional mass of the object
The measuring equipment must have made an error in tracking the energy

en_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms; friction and air resistance convert the mechanical energy into heat and sound energy that dissipates into the surroundings.
en_l3_t2.realPurpose: This principle explains why no machine can be perfectly efficient forever and why engineers must account for energy 'losses' as heat when designing motors, vehicles and machinery.

en_l2_t3.questionTemplate: A machine does {{work}} J of work in {{time}} seconds. What is its power output? (Power = Work ÷ Time, measured in watts)
en_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Power measures how quickly work is done or energy is transferred, so dividing the total work by the time taken tells you the average rate of energy transfer per second.
en_l2_t3.realPurpose: Power ratings (like those on light bulbs or motors, measured in watts) let consumers and engineers compare how quickly different devices use or produce energy.

en_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A force of {{force}} N is used to push an object a distance of {{distance}} m in the direction of the force. How much work is done? (Work = Force × Distance)
en_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Work in physics has a precise meaning: it is done only when a force causes movement in the direction of that force, and its amount is calculated simply as force multiplied by the distance moved.
en_l2_t4.realPurpose: This precise definition of work is the foundation for calculating energy transfer in machines, from simple levers to engines that move vehicles.

variants.question: A student pushes very hard against a heavy wall for {{minutes}} minutes, but the wall does not move at all. The student claims they did "a huge amount of work" because they tried so hard. What is the physics mistake here?
variants.answer: In physics, work is only done when a force causes an object to actually move some distance in the direction of the force; since the wall didn't move at all, zero physical work was done on the wall, no matter how much effort or energy the student felt they exerted
distractors: The student is correct — pushing hard for a long time always counts as a large amount of physical work, whether or not anything moves
Work was done, but only a very small amount, roughly proportional to how tired the student felt afterward
Work can only be measured by how long an activity lasts, regardless of whether any force or movement was involved

en_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: The everyday meaning of 'work' (feeling effort or getting tired) is different from the precise physics definition, which requires an actual displacement in the direction of an applied force; since Work = Force × Distance, any situation with zero distance moved results in exactly zero work, regardless of the force applied or the effort felt.
en_l3_t3.realPurpose: This precise distinction prevents confusion when calculating real energy transfers in machines and systems, where only forces that actually cause motion contribute useful work.

variants.question: A student believes a 100% energy-efficient machine (one that wastes absolutely no energy as heat) could be built if engineers just tried hard enough. What is the more accurate physics understanding here?
variants.answer: Due to friction and other unavoidable energy losses (often as heat), no real machine can be 100% efficient; the Law of Conservation of Energy means no energy is destroyed, but useful energy is unavoidably converted into less useful forms like heat during every real energy transfer
distractors: The student is correct — a sufficiently well-engineered machine could theoretically achieve 100% efficiency with no energy losses at all
100% efficient machines already exist and are commonly used in industry today
Efficiency losses only occur in electrical machines, never in purely mechanical ones

en_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Friction between moving parts, electrical resistance, and air resistance are all unavoidable in real physical systems, and each one converts some portion of useful input energy into heat that then spreads into the surroundings and becomes very difficult to recover and reuse.
en_l3_t4.realPurpose: Understanding this real-world limit drives engineers to continually seek out lower-friction designs and better materials, even though the theoretical ideal of 100% efficiency can never actually be reached.

variants.question: What is the SI unit of both work and energy?
What is the SI unit of power?

en_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Work and energy share the same unit (the joule) since energy is simply the capacity to do work, while power has its own distinct unit (the watt), because it also factors in the time taken.
en_l1_t5.realPurpose: Knowing these units by heart makes it possible to instantly check whether a stated answer to a work, energy or power problem is even dimensionally plausible.

variants.question: Which formula is used to calculate work done?
Which formula is used to calculate power?

en_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Work multiplies the applied force by the distance moved in the force's direction, while power divides the total work done by the time taken to do it, giving the rate of energy transfer.
en_l1_t6.realPurpose: These two formulas are the foundation for every subsequent numeric problem involving force, distance, work, time or power.

variants.question: For work to be done on an object, in the precise physics sense, what must happen?
variants.answer: A force must cause the object to actually move some distance in the direction of that force
distractors: Any force must be applied, whether or not the object actually moves
The object must become noticeably warmer as a result of the force
The object's mass must increase as a result of the force

en_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: The physics definition of work is strict: it requires an actual displacement in the direction of the applied force, so a force that produces no movement at all does zero work, no matter how large that force is.
en_l1_t7.realPurpose: This precise requirement is what separates the everyday, effort-based idea of 'work' from the physics quantity used in real energy calculations.

variants.question: What is kinetic energy?
variants.answer: The energy possessed by an object because of its motion

variants.question: What is potential energy?
variants.answer: The energy possessed by an object because of its position, height, or state of strain

distractorPool: The energy possessed by an object because of its motion
The energy possessed by an object because of its position, height, or state of strain
The energy released only when a substance is burned
The energy stored only inside electrical batteries
en_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Kinetic energy depends purely on an object's motion (its mass and velocity), while potential energy depends on an object's configuration relative to a reference, such as its height above the ground or how far a spring is stretched.
en_l1_t8.realPurpose: These two definitions form the basis of every mechanical energy calculation, from a falling object's changing energy to a compressed spring's stored energy.

variants.question: Which of these correctly gives the formula for kinetic energy?
distractors: KE = mass × velocity²
KE = mass × velocity
KE = ½ × mass × velocity

en_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: The kinetic energy formula includes both the one-half factor and the squaring of velocity; dropping either part, as the listed distractors do, produces a value that no longer matches the true kinetic energy.
en_l1_t9.realPurpose: Memorising this formula precisely (including the one-half factor and the square on velocity) is essential before attempting any numeric kinetic energy calculation.

variants.question: Which of these correctly gives the formula for gravitational potential energy?
distractors: PE = mass × height
PE = mass × g
PE = g × height

en_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Gravitational potential energy depends on all three of mass, the gravitational field strength (g), and height; omitting any one of these three factors, as each distractor does, gives an incomplete and incorrect formula.
en_l1_t10.realPurpose: Recalling this formula precisely is essential for correctly calculating the stored energy in any object raised against gravity, from a lifted weight to water stored in a dam.

variants.question: Between two machines that both do the exact same amount of work, the one that finishes in LESS time has...
distractors: A lower power output
Exactly the same power output as the slower machine
No power output at all, since power only applies to electrical devices

en_l1_t11.technicalIntricacy: Since power is work divided by time, doing the same amount of work in less time means dividing by a smaller number, which always results in a larger power value.
en_l1_t11.realPurpose: This comparison is exactly how machines and engines are rated and compared in practice, since power measures how quickly useful work gets done, not just how much.

variants.question: A ceiling fan converts electrical energy into which primary useful form of energy?
distractors: Potential energy
Chemical energy
Nuclear energy

en_l1_t12.technicalIntricacy: A ceiling fan's motor converts incoming electrical energy mainly into the kinetic energy of its spinning blades, with a smaller unwanted portion lost as heat in the motor.
en_l1_t12.realPurpose: Identifying a device's main useful energy conversion is the basis for evaluating how efficiently it turns input energy into the output it was actually designed to provide.

en_l2_t5.questionTemplate: A ball of mass {{mass}} kg is thrown with a velocity of {{velocity}} m/s. What is its kinetic energy? (KE = ½ × mass × velocity²)
en_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Kinetic energy grows with the square of velocity, so doubling a thrown ball's speed actually quadruples its kinetic energy rather than simply doubling it.
en_l2_t5.realPurpose: This calculation shows why even a modest increase in a thrown or moving object's speed can carry a disproportionately large increase in impact energy.

en_l2_t6.questionTemplate: A book of mass {{mass}} kg sits on a shelf {{height}} m above the floor. What is its potential energy relative to the floor? (Take g = 10 m/s², PE = mass × g × height)
en_l2_t6.technicalIntricacy: Gravitational potential energy multiplies mass, the gravitational field strength, and height together; leaving out the gravitational field strength (as the listed alternate does) understates the true stored energy.
en_l2_t6.realPurpose: This calculation shows how much energy would be released as kinetic energy if the book fell from the shelf, since its potential energy converts directly into kinetic energy during the fall.

en_l2_t7.questionTemplate: A force of {{force}} N does {{work}} J of work on an object. Over what distance did the force act? (Distance = Work ÷ Force)
en_l2_t7.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging Work = Force × Distance shows that distance can be found by dividing the work done by the force applied, since a larger force needs to act over a proportionally shorter distance to achieve the same total work.
en_l2_t7.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used whenever the distance moved needs to be worked out from a known force and a known amount of work done, such as analysing a lever or a simple machine.

variants.question: A student believes that using a LARGER force to push a box across the floor always means MORE work is done, regardless of the distance moved. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Work depends on both force AND distance (Work = Force × Distance); a larger force applied over a shorter distance can actually result in LESS work than a smaller force applied over a longer distance
distractors: The student is correct — work depends only on the amount of force used, never on the distance moved
Work depends only on the time taken, regardless of the force or distance involved
