lt_l1_t16.realPurpose: Diffuse reflection off rough surfaces (like paper, walls and clothing) is what allows us to see ordinary objects clearly from many different angles, unlike a mirror, which only shows a clear image from specific angles.

variants.question: At what angle are the two mirrors inside a simple periscope tilted, relative to the tube?

lt_l1_t17.technicalIntricacy: Setting each mirror at exactly 45° means a horizontal incoming ray is reflected through a 90° turn down the tube, and the second mirror at 45° turns it another 90° back to horizontal, delivering the image to the viewer's eye.
lt_l1_t17.realPurpose: This precise mirror angle is what makes real periscopes, used in submarines and to see over crowds, function correctly.

variants.question: An image that cannot be captured or formed on a screen, and only appears to exist behind a mirror, is called a:
An image that CAN be captured or formed on a screen, such as one formed by a camera lens, is called a:

lt_l1_t18.technicalIntricacy: A virtual image forms where reflected (or refracted) rays only appear to diverge from, without light rays actually meeting there, so it cannot be projected onto a screen; a real image forms where light rays actually converge and meet, so it can be captured on a screen.
lt_l1_t18.realPurpose: This distinction explains why you cannot photograph the image seen in a plane mirror directly off a screen placed behind the mirror, while a real image, like the one formed inside a camera, can be captured on film or a sensor.

variants.question: Which type of mirror converges (brings together) a beam of parallel light rays after reflection?
Which type of mirror diverges (spreads out) a beam of parallel light rays after reflection?

lt_l1_t19.technicalIntricacy: A concave mirror curves inward like the inside of a bowl, which causes reflected parallel rays to converge toward a single focal point; a convex mirror curves outward, causing reflected parallel rays to spread apart as if diverging from a point behind the mirror.
lt_l1_t19.realPurpose: This converging or diverging behaviour is the basic optical property that determines whether a curved mirror is useful for concentrating light (as in a torch or solar cooker) or for widening a field of view (as in a vehicle mirror).

variants.question: What is the name given to the exact point on a mirror's surface where an incident ray strikes it?

lt_l1_t20.technicalIntricacy: The point of incidence is the single, specific location on a reflecting surface where an incoming ray of light meets the surface; both the angle of incidence and angle of reflection are measured from the normal drawn at exactly this point.
lt_l1_t20.realPurpose: Precisely identifying the point of incidence is the essential first step in accurately drawing or calculating any ray diagram involving reflection.

lt_l2_t8.questionTemplate: An object stands {{distance}} cm in front of a plane mirror. It then moves {{move}} cm closer to the mirror. What is the new total distance between the object and its image (measuring straight through the mirror)?

lt_l2_t8.realPurpose: Recalculating this total distance after the object moves shows how a plane mirror's image continuously tracks the object's position, always maintaining the same equal-distance relationship.

lt_l2_t9.questionTemplate: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of {{angle}}° (measured from the normal). What is the total angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray? (This total angle = 180° − 2 × angle of incidence)
lt_l2_t9.technicalIntricacy: Since the reflected ray makes the same angle with the normal as the incident ray, the total angle swept between the incident and reflected rays is what remains of a straight 180° line after removing both of these equal angles, giving 180° − 2 × angle of incidence.
lt_l2_t9.realPurpose: This exact relationship is why a mirror tilted at precisely 45° turns a beam of light through a full 90°, the principle used to build a working periscope.

lt_l2_t10.questionTemplate: Two separate objects are placed in front of the same plane mirror, at distances of {{d1}} cm and {{d2}} cm. What is the difference between the distances of their two images from the mirror?

lt_l2_t10.realPurpose: This equal-distance property means the relative spacing between multiple objects is exactly preserved in their mirror images, which matters when precisely designing optical instruments using multiple reflected images.

variants.question: A student believes that if an object is placed very close to a convex mirror, the mirror will start forming a magnified, real image, just like a concave mirror does. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

lt_l3_t6.realPurpose: Understanding this consistent behaviour is why convex mirrors are reliably used for wide-view applications like vehicle mirrors and security mirrors, where a predictable, always-smaller image is actually the desired effect.

variants.question: What is the term for a substance changing from a solid to a liquid due to heat?

he_l1_t4.realPurpose: Latent heat explains why ice at 0°C takes a noticeable amount of time to fully melt into water, even though heat is continuously being supplied throughout that time.

variants.question: Which of these best describes 'heat' in physics?

variants.question: Why is it unsafe to completely fill a rigid, sealed bottle with liquid and then leave it somewhere it might heat up?

he_l2_t1.questionTemplate: A liquid cools down from {{initialTemp}}°C to {{finalTemp}}°C. What is the total fall in temperature?

he_l2_t2.questionTemplate: A metal block's temperature rises by {{rise1}}°C during the first stage of heating, and then by a further {{rise2}}°C during a second stage of heating. What is the TOTAL rise in temperature over both stages combined?

he_l2_t3.questionTemplate: A container of water starts at {{startTemp}}°C and is heated so that its temperature rises steadily by {{ratePerMin}}°C every minute. Assuming no change of state occurs, what will its temperature be after {{minutes}} minutes of heating?

he_l2_t4.questionTemplate: Two metal blocks are placed in contact: one starts at {{temp1}}°C and the other at {{temp2}}°C. Heat will flow from the hotter block to the colder one until they reach the same temperature. What is the difference between their starting temperatures?

variants.question: On the Fahrenheit scale, at what temperature does water freeze?

variants.question: What is the name for the theoretical lowest possible temperature, equal to 0 K (about −273°C), at which particles have minimal thermal energy?

variants.question: Which type of thermometer is specifically designed with a narrow temperature range to measure human body temperature?

tm_l1_t5.realPurpose: This specialised design lets a clinical thermometer detect even small, medically significant changes in body temperature, such as a mild fever.

variants.question: Which liquid has traditionally been used inside many thermometers because it expands evenly with temperature and does not stick to glass?

tm_l1_t6.realPurpose: Understanding why mercury was chosen for traditional thermometers highlights the specific physical properties (even expansion, no sticking, a wide liquid range) that make a substance suitable for precise temperature measurement.

variants.question: What is the normal average human body temperature, commonly cited on the Celsius scale?
What is the normal average human body temperature, commonly cited on the Fahrenheit scale?

variants.question: Which two temperature scales have degree intervals of exactly the same size, differing from each other only by a fixed offset of 273?

variants.question: Which of these is closest to typical room temperature?

tm_l2_t3.questionTemplate: A mercury thermometer's stem between the ice point (0°C) and the steam point (100°C) measures {{totalLength}} mm long, and is divided into 100 equal degree divisions. What is the length of stem representing each 1°C division?

variants.answer: The distance between two consecutive, identical points on the wave (such as one compression to the next)
distractors: The total distance the sound travels before fading out completely
The time taken for one complete vibration
The maximum pressure reached during a compression

rs_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: Wavelength specifically measures the physical length of one complete wave cycle in space, distinct from frequency, which counts cycles per second, and time period, which measures the duration of one cycle.
rs_l1_t7.realPurpose: A precise definition of wavelength is essential for correctly applying the Speed = Frequency × Wavelength formula and for comparing different types of waves.

variants.question: Which of these applications relies on ultrasonic sound (frequency above 20,000 Hz)?
variants.answer: Medical ultrasound imaging of internal organs

variants.question: Which of these natural phenomena typically involves infrasonic sound (frequency below 20 Hz)?
variants.answer: Communication between elephants over long distances

distractorPool: Medical ultrasound imaging of internal organs
Communication between elephants over long distances
A typical human conversation at a normal volume
rs_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Ultrasonic and infrasonic sound both lie outside the range of human hearing, yet each has distinct real-world sources and applications: ultrasonic waves for detailed imaging and cleaning, and infrasonic waves for long-distance animal communication and detecting large-scale natural events.
rs_l1_t8.realPurpose: This connects the abstract frequency ranges of ultrasonic and infrasonic sound to concrete, well-known real-world examples of each.

rs_l2_t1.questionTemplate: A sound wave has a frequency of {{frequency}} Hz and a wavelength of {{wavelength}} m. What is its speed? (Speed = Frequency × Wavelength)
rs_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging Speed = Frequency × Wavelength shows that speed can be calculated directly once both frequency and wavelength are known, simply by multiplying them together.
rs_l2_t1.realPurpose: This calculation is used whenever a wave's frequency and physical wavelength have been measured separately, to determine how fast the wave itself is actually travelling.

rs_l2_t2.questionTemplate: A sound wave travels at {{speed}} m/s and has a wavelength of {{wavelength}} m. What is its frequency? (Frequency = Speed ÷ Wavelength)
rs_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging Speed = Frequency × Wavelength the other way shows that frequency can be found by dividing the wave's speed by its wavelength.
rs_l2_t2.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used whenever a wave's speed and physical wavelength are known but its vibration frequency needs to be determined.

variants.question: A student stands about {{dist}} metres from a wall and shouts loudly, expecting to hear a clear, separate echo, but hears only a slightly prolonged sound instead. What is the mistake in the student's expectation?
variants.answer: At just {{dist}} m from the wall, the reflected sound completes its round trip in far less than 0.1 seconds, the minimum gap the ear needs to perceive a separate echo, so it simply blends with the original sound instead of being heard as a distinct echo — a much greater distance (roughly 17 m or more) is needed for a true echo
distractors: The wall must not be a solid enough material to reflect any sound at all
Echoes can never be heard indoors or near any solid structure, no matter the distance
The student's shout was not loud enough to produce a measurable echo at this or any distance

rs_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Hearing a distinct echo requires the reflected sound to arrive at least about 0.1 seconds after the direct sound; since sound travels at roughly 340 m/s, this requires a reflecting surface to be at least about 17 metres away, so echoes cannot be perceived at short distances no matter how loud the shout is.
rs_l3_t1.realPurpose: This calculation explains why echoes are common against distant cliffs or across large halls, but never occur when speaking close to a nearby wall.

variants.question: What is the 'directive property' of a magnet?
variants.answer: A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest pointing in a north-south direction

variants.question: What is the 'attractive property' of a magnet?
variants.answer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt towards itself

variants.question: Where is a magnet's attractive force concentrated, being weakest at its centre?

distractorPool: A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest pointing in a north-south direction
A magnet attracts magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt towards itself
A magnet loses its magnetism permanently the moment it attracts an object
A magnet's strength is the same at every point along its length, including the centre
mg_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: A magnet has several defining properties beyond just its two laws: it aligns itself along north-south when freely suspended, it attracts magnetic materials, and its magnetic effect is concentrated at its poles rather than spread evenly.
mg_l1_t2.realPurpose: These basic properties are what allow magnets to be used in compasses, through the directive property, and in sorting or lifting magnetic materials, through the attractive property concentrated at the poles.

variants.question: Is nickel a magnetic material or a non-magnetic material?
Is cobalt a magnetic material or a non-magnetic material?
Is steel a magnetic material or a non-magnetic material?
Is aluminium a magnetic material or a non-magnetic material?
Is copper a magnetic material or a non-magnetic material?
Is plastic a magnetic material or a non-magnetic material?

distractorPool: A material with no atomic structure
mg_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Only a small group of materials, mainly iron, nickel, cobalt, steel and their alloys, are magnetic; many other metals, such as aluminium and copper, are not magnetic at all, despite being good electrical conductors.
mg_l1_t3.realPurpose: Knowing that not all metals are magnetic, aluminium and copper being common examples, prevents a very common mix-up between 'metal' and 'magnetic material'.

variants.question: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do magnetic field lines conventionally point?
variants.answer: From the north pole to the south pole

variants.question: What happens if you try to draw two magnetic field lines crossing each other?
variants.answer: They never actually cross — magnetic field lines never intersect

variants.question: Where are a bar magnet's field lines most closely spaced, indicating the strongest field?

distractorPool: From the north pole to the south pole
They never actually cross — magnetic field lines never intersect
From the south pole to the north pole, both inside and outside the magnet
Magnetic field lines regularly cross each other at the magnet's centre
Field lines are evenly spaced everywhere, showing the field is equally strong throughout
mg_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Magnetic field lines are a way of visualising the direction and strength of a magnetic field: they run from north to south outside the magnet, are always closer together (denser) near the poles where the field is strongest, and never cross because the field has only one direction at any given point.
mg_l1_t4.realPurpose: Field line diagrams let scientists and students predict how a compass needle or another magnet will behave at any position around a magnet, without needing complex measurements.

variants.question: Which simple instrument is used to trace and detect the direction of a magnetic field?
distractors: A voltmeter
A thermometer
A barometer

mg_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: A compass needle is itself a small, freely pivoting magnet, so it aligns with and reveals the direction of any external magnetic field it is placed within, tracing out the field's shape point by point.
mg_l1_t5.realPurpose: This simple technique is exactly how the classic magnetic field line diagrams around a bar magnet are experimentally plotted in a school laboratory.

variants.question: What is an electromagnet?
variants.answer: A temporary magnet created by passing an electric current through a coil of wire, often wound around a soft iron core
distractors: A permanent magnet made from naturally magnetic rock
A magnet that only works when its coil is disconnected from any power source
A device that converts magnetism directly into light

mg_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet's magnetism exists only while current flows through its coil, since the current itself is what generates the magnetic field, usually made stronger by winding the coil around a soft iron core.
mg_l1_t6.realPurpose: This on-demand, switchable magnetism is why electromagnets, not permanent magnets, are used in devices like cranes, doorbells and electric motors, where magnetism needs to be turned on and off.

variants.question: Which of these changes would increase the strength of an electromagnet?
variants.answer: Increasing the number of turns of wire in the coil

variants.question: Which of these changes would also increase the strength of an electromagnet?
variants.answer: Increasing the current flowing through the coil

variants.question: Which of these changes would also increase the strength of an electromagnet?
variants.answer: Adding a soft iron core inside the coil

distractorPool: Increasing the number of turns of wire in the coil
Increasing the current flowing through the coil
Adding a soft iron core inside the coil
Winding the coil around a non-magnetic wooden core instead of an iron one
Disconnecting the coil from its power source
mg_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: An electromagnet's strength depends on three controllable factors: the number of turns in its coil, the amount of current flowing through it, and whether it has a soft iron core to concentrate its magnetic field.
mg_l1_t7.realPurpose: Engineers adjust these three factors together to design electromagnets suited to different tasks, from a gentle desk toy to an industrial crane lifting scrap metal.

variants.question: Which of these actions can cause a permanent magnet to lose its magnetism?
variants.answer: Heating it strongly, or hammering/dropping it repeatedly
distractors: Keeping it perfectly still in a drawer for a few minutes
Bringing it near another magnet's like pole, without any impact or heat
Measuring its magnetic field strength with a compass

mg_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: Strong heat or repeated mechanical shocks disturb the orderly alignment of a magnet's internal magnetic domains, scrambling them back into a random arrangement and weakening or destroying its magnetism.
mg_l1_t8.realPurpose: Knowing this explains why permanent magnets must be stored and handled carefully, away from heat sources and rough impacts, to preserve their magnetism for as long as possible.

variants.question: What happens when a piece of unmagnetised iron is brought close to (but not touching) a strong magnet?
variants.answer: The iron itself becomes temporarily magnetised, through a process called magnetic induction
distractors: Nothing happens at all unless the iron directly touches the magnet
The iron becomes permanently magnetised forever, even after being moved far away
The original magnet immediately loses all of its own magnetism

mg_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: A magnet's field can realign the internal domains of a nearby magnetic material even without contact, temporarily turning that material into a weak magnet itself, a process called magnetic induction, which is actually why magnetic materials are attracted to magnets in the first place.
mg_l1_t9.realPurpose: Magnetic induction explains why a paperclip can pick up other paperclips after touching a magnet, and is a key step in understanding exactly how attraction between a magnet and a magnetic material works.

mg_l2_t1.questionTemplate: An electromagnet's magnetic strength is directly proportional to the current flowing through its coil (for a fixed number of turns). If the current is increased from {{current1}} A to {{current2}} A, by what factor does the magnetic strength increase?
mg_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Just as with the number of turns, magnetic strength is directly proportional to the current flowing through the coil, holding turns fixed, so multiplying the current by a given factor multiplies the magnetic strength by that exact same factor.
mg_l2_t1.realPurpose: This is why devices needing a very strong electromagnet, like industrial lifting magnets, are supplied with a large, carefully controlled electric current.

mg_l2_t2.questionTemplate: If you have {{numMagnets}} separate bar magnets, how many magnetic poles are there in total?
mg_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Since every magnet, no matter its size, always has exactly one north pole and one south pole, the total number of poles among several separate magnets is simply twice the number of magnets.
mg_l2_t2.realPurpose: This directly applies the Second Law of Magnetism, that poles always exist in pairs, to a countable, concrete scenario.

mg_l2_t3.questionTemplate: Magnet A can lift a maximum of {{massA}} g of iron filings, and Magnet B can lift a maximum of {{massB}} g. If both magnets are used together and their lifting forces simply add up, what is the maximum total mass they could lift together?
mg_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: When two magnets act together on the same object, their individual attractive forces combine, so the maximum combined lifting capacity is found by simply adding each magnet's individual lifting capacity.
mg_l2_t3.realPurpose: This is why multiple magnets are sometimes combined in industrial lifting equipment or magnetic separators, to achieve a greater combined attractive force than any single magnet could provide alone.

mg_l2_t4.questionTemplate: Magnet A can lift {{massA}} g while Magnet B, made of the same material but larger, can lift {{massB}} g. How many times stronger is Magnet B compared to Magnet A?
mg_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Comparing two magnets' lifting capacities as a ratio, rather than a difference, shows how many times stronger one magnet is relative to the other, found by dividing the larger capacity by the smaller one.
mg_l2_t4.realPurpose: Expressing magnet strength as a multiple, rather than just a raw number, makes it easy to compare magnets of very different sizes on a common scale.

variants.question: In a circuit diagram, what does the symbol of two parallel lines, one longer, one shorter, usually represent?
variants.answer: A cell (with the longer line as the positive terminal and the shorter line as the negative terminal)

variants.question: In a circuit diagram, what does a circle with a small cross or loop inside it usually represent?
In a circuit diagram, what does a small gap or break in the wire, that a switch can open or close, usually represent?

distractorPool: A cell (with the longer line as the positive terminal and the shorter line as the negative terminal)
A resistor (a component that limits current)
A fuse (a safety component that breaks the circuit under excess current)
An ammeter (a device that measures current)
ec_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Standardised circuit symbols let anyone read a circuit diagram consistently, without needing to draw a realistic picture of every wire and component.
ec_l1_t1.realPurpose: Recognising standard circuit symbols is essential for understanding textbook circuit diagrams and for correctly interpreting and communicating circuit designs.

variants.question: What is a 'closed circuit'?
variants.answer: A complete, unbroken path that allows current to flow continuously around it

variants.question: What is an 'open circuit'?
variants.answer: A circuit with a break somewhere in its path, so no current can flow at all

distractorPool: A complete, unbroken path that allows current to flow continuously around it
A circuit with a break somewhere in its path, so no current can flow at all
A circuit that only works with alternating current, never direct current
A circuit containing more than one cell connected in parallel
ec_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Current can only flow when there is a complete, unbroken conducting path from one terminal of the source, through the components, and back to the other terminal; any break anywhere in that path makes it an open circuit, stopping current everywhere.
ec_l1_t2.realPurpose: This distinction explains exactly what a switch does: it deliberately opens or closes the circuit's path to control whether current can flow.

variants.question: Is a graphite (pencil lead) rod a good conductor of electricity or an insulator?
Is saltwater a good conductor of electricity or an insulator?
Is dry paper a good conductor of electricity or an insulator?
Is dry cotton cloth a good conductor of electricity or an insulator?

distractorPool: A semiconductor only at high temperatures
ec_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Electrical conduction isn't limited to metals: graphite, a non-metal, and saltwater, due to dissolved ions, both conduct electricity well, while ordinary dry materials like paper and cotton lack free charge carriers and resist current flow.
ec_l1_t3.realPurpose: Recognising that some non-metals conduct electricity, and that even a liquid like water needs dissolved substances to conduct well, rounds out a fuller, more accurate picture of electrical conduction.

variants.question: What is 'electric current'?
variants.answer: The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A)

variants.question: What is 'voltage' (also called potential difference)?
variants.answer: The electrical 'push' that drives current around a circuit, measured in volts (V)

variants.question: What is 'resistance'?
variants.answer: A material's opposition to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms (Ω)

distractorPool: The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A)
The electrical 'push' that drives current around a circuit, measured in volts (V)
A material's opposition to the flow of electric current, measured in ohms (Ω)
The total amount of electrical energy stored in a cell, measured in joules
The physical length of wire used in a circuit, measured in metres
ec_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Current, voltage and resistance are three distinct but related quantities describing a circuit, how much charge flows, what drives that flow, and what opposes it, and together they're connected by the formula V = I × R.
ec_l1_t4.realPurpose: Clearly defining these three basic quantities is essential before they can be meaningfully combined in circuit calculations.

variants.question: In a series circuit, how are components connected relative to each other?
variants.answer: One after another, along a single path, so the same current flows through each

variants.question: In a parallel circuit, how are components connected relative to each other?
variants.answer: Side by side, in separate branches, each connected directly across the same two points

distractorPool: One after another, along a single path, so the same current flows through each
Side by side, in separate branches, each connected directly across the same two points
Components in series are always connected in separate branches
Components in parallel always share a single current path
ec_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: The defining structural difference between series and parallel is simple: series components form one single continuous path end-to-end, while parallel components each form their own separate branch connected across common points.
ec_l1_t5.realPurpose: Recognising this structural difference at a glance is the first step in correctly analysing or sketching any circuit diagram, before calculating current or voltage in it.

variants.question: What is the role of a connecting wire in an electric circuit?
variants.answer: To provide a conducting path that carries current between the different components of the circuit
distractors: To store electric charge for later use, like a cell
To automatically break the circuit if too much current flows, like a fuse
To measure how much current is flowing through the circuit

ec_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Connecting wires are usually made of a good conductor like copper, often coated in an insulating layer, and their sole job is to complete the conducting path linking every other component together.
ec_l1_t6.realPurpose: Without connecting wires providing this continuous conducting path, none of a circuit's other components, however well designed, could actually function together.

variants.question: How does an electric bulb (lamp) produce light in a circuit?
variants.answer: Current flowing through its thin resistive filament heats it until it glows, converting electrical energy into light and heat
distractors: The bulb chemically reacts with the surrounding air to produce light
The bulb stores light energy in advance and releases it slowly over time
The bulb's glass casing itself is what produces the glow, not the filament

ec_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: A bulb's thin filament has enough electrical resistance that the current flowing through it generates significant heat, and at high enough temperatures, that heated filament glows and emits visible light.
ec_l1_t7.realPurpose: Understanding this is why a burnt-out bulb, with a broken filament, creates an open circuit; no current can pass through the gap where the filament has failed.

ec_l2_t1.questionTemplate: A circuit has a resistance of {{resistance}} Ω and a voltage of {{voltage}} V across it. What is the current flowing through it? (I = V ÷ R)
ec_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging V = I × R shows that current can be found by dividing voltage by resistance; for a fixed voltage, a higher resistance always results in a smaller current.
ec_l2_t1.realPurpose: This rearranged formula is used whenever a component's resistance and the voltage across it are known, but the current flowing through it needs to be found.

ec_l2_t2.questionTemplate: A circuit has a current of {{current}} A flowing through it when a voltage of {{voltage}} V is applied across it. What is its resistance? (R = V ÷ I)
ec_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging V = I × R the other way shows that resistance can be found by dividing the voltage across a component by the current flowing through it.
ec_l2_t2.realPurpose: This rearranged formula lets engineers determine an unknown component's resistance directly from simple voltage and current measurements, without needing to inspect the component itself.

variants.question: A student wires two bulbs on separate parallel branches, with a switch placed only in the branch containing Bulb 1. The student expects that turning this switch off will also turn off Bulb 2. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Since each branch of a parallel circuit is an independent current path, a switch placed only in Bulb 1's branch only breaks that one branch; Bulb 2, on its own separate branch, keeps receiving current and stays lit regardless of Bulb 1's switch
distractors: The student is correct — a switch anywhere in a parallel circuit always breaks current to every branch
Both bulbs will turn off, but only because parallel circuits always share a single switch by design
Neither bulb will turn off, since switches have no effect at all in parallel circuits

ec_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: A switch only interrupts the specific branch it is wired into; because parallel branches are electrically independent paths back to the source, a switch's effect never spreads to a different, unswitched branch.
ec_l3_t1.realPurpose: This is exactly why independent switches for different lights or appliances are wired into their own separate parallel branches, so each can be controlled without affecting the others.

area_measurement.title: Area and Its Measurement
area_measurement.overview: Area is a derived quantity that measures the amount of two-dimensional surface a shape covers. This chapter covers the SI units used for area, common measuring instruments, and how to calculate the area of simple shapes like rectangles.
area_measurement.deepDivePurpose: Accurately measuring and calculating area is essential for countless real-world tasks, from buying the right amount of flooring or paint to calculating land size for construction and agriculture.
recap: Area is a derived quantity, found by combining length measurements, and is expressed in square units such as cm² or m².
The area of a rectangle is calculated as length × breadth.
Common instruments like a metre scale, measuring tape, or vernier callipers are used to measure the lengths needed to calculate area.
Precision matters: recording more decimal places than an instrument's least count allows creates false precision in an area calculation.
Converting an area between units (e.g., m² to cm²) requires squaring the linear conversion factor, not applying it directly.

volume_measurement.title: Volume and Its Measurement
volume_measurement.overview: Volume measures the amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies. This chapter covers the SI units used for volume, and how to measure the volume of both regular solids (using formulas) and irregular solids (using the displacement method).
volume_measurement.deepDivePurpose: The displacement method for measuring irregular volumes is a foundational experimental technique in science, letting us measure objects, like stones or small parts, that no simple formula could otherwise handle.
recap: Volume is a derived quantity, expressed in cubic units such as cm³ or m³, or in related liquid units like millilitres and litres.
The volume of a regular solid, like a cuboid, can be calculated using a formula (length × breadth × height).
The volume of an irregularly shaped solid is measured using the displacement method: submerging it in a measuring cylinder and recording the rise in water level.
For the displacement method to work correctly, the object must be fully submerged in the liquid.
Mass can be found from volume and density (Mass = Density × Volume), and volume can be found from mass and density (Volume = Mass ÷ Density).

density_speed.title: Measurement of Density and Speed
density_speed.overview: Density and speed are both derived quantities, formed by dividing one fundamental (or derived) quantity by another. This chapter covers calculating density from mass and volume, and revisits how fundamental and derived quantities combine to form these everyday measurements.
density_speed.deepDivePurpose: Density calculations let scientists identify unknown materials and predict whether objects float or sink, while understanding how derived quantities are built from fundamentals is the basis of dimensional reasoning throughout physics.
recap: A derived quantity is formed by combining fundamental quantities through multiplication or division, without introducing a new base unit.
Density = Mass ÷ Volume, measured in units like g/cm³ or kg/m³.
Speed = Distance ÷ Time, measured in units like m/s.
Density calculations must use consistent units for mass and volume (e.g., both in grams and cm³) to give a meaningful result.
Rearranging the density formula allows mass to be found from density and volume, or volume to be found from mass and density.

rest_motion.title: Rest and Motion: Kinds of Motion
rest_motion.overview: An object is at rest if its position doesn't change relative to a reference point, and in motion if it does. This chapter covers the different kinds of motion — rectilinear, circular, rotatory and oscillatory — the distinction between uniform and non-uniform motion, and the distinction between mass and weight.
rest_motion.deepDivePurpose: Recognising different kinds of motion is the starting point for analysing how anything moves, from a car on a highway to a fan's spinning blades, and underlies the design of machines that rely on a specific type of motion.
recap: An object is at rest if its position does not change with respect to a reference point over time, and in motion if it does.

Rectilinear motion is motion in a straight line; circular motion follows a curved, closed path; rotatory motion is spinning about a fixed internal axis; oscillatory motion is repeating back-and-forth motion.
Uniform motion covers equal distances in equal time intervals; non-uniform motion covers unequal distances in equal time intervals.
Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between a start and end position, and can be zero even if the total distance travelled is not.
An object moving at constant speed but continuously changing direction (like in circular motion) is still accelerating, since velocity includes direction.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object (measured in kilograms) and never changes with location; weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass (measured in newtons, Weight = Mass × g) and changes if gravity changes.

speed_velocity.title: Speed and Velocity
speed_velocity.overview: Speed measures how fast an object moves, while velocity measures both how fast and in what direction. This chapter covers calculating speed and distance, converting between units like m/s and km/h, and understanding acceleration as the rate of change of velocity.
speed_velocity.deepDivePurpose: Distinguishing speed from velocity, and understanding acceleration, is essential for correctly analysing motion in any direction-sensitive context, from sports science to vehicle safety design.
recap: Speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only); velocity is a vector quantity that also specifies direction.
Average speed = Total distance ÷ Total time; this differs from simply averaging two different speeds over unequal times.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time, and can result from a change in speed, a change in direction, or both.
Converting between m/s and km/h uses the fixed factor 3.6, since 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.
Calculations involving speed, distance and time must always use consistent units before dividing or multiplying.

energy_work.title: Energy, Work and Their Units
energy_work.overview: Work is done when a force causes an object to move in the direction of that force, and energy is the capacity to do work. This chapter covers calculating work and power, and the SI units used to measure them.
energy_work.deepDivePurpose: The precise physics definition of work — requiring actual movement in the direction of a force — explains why effort alone (like pushing against an immovable wall) does not always count as work, a subtlety essential to correctly analysing machines and energy transfer.
recap: Work is done only when a force causes an object to move some distance in the direction of that force; Work = Force × Distance.
The SI unit of work and energy is the joule (J).
Power measures how quickly work is done, calculated as Power = Work ÷ Time.
Kinetic energy (energy of motion) and potential energy (energy of position) are both forms of mechanical energy, each with their own calculation formula.
No real machine can be 100% efficient, since some energy is always lost as heat due to friction and other unavoidable losses.

various_forms_energy.title: Various Forms of Energy and Their Interconversion
various_forms_energy.overview: Energy exists in many forms — mechanical, heat, light, sound, chemical and electrical — and can be transformed from one form into another, though the total amount of energy never changes. This chapter covers identifying energy transformations and the Law of Conservation of Energy.
various_forms_energy.deepDivePurpose: Understanding how energy converts between forms explains how every energy-using device works, from a solar panel converting light to electricity, to a swinging pendulum converting potential energy to kinetic energy and back.
recap: Common forms of energy include mechanical (kinetic and potential), heat, light, sound, chemical, and electrical energy.
Every energy-using device converts one form of energy into another, often losing some as heat in the process.
The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms.
Renewable energy sources (like solar and wind) are naturally replenished, while non-renewable sources (like coal and petroleum) are used up far faster than they can form.
When a pendulum or bouncing ball appears to 'lose' energy over time, that energy has actually converted into heat and sound due to friction and air resistance.

light_terms.title: Light and Terms Used to Understand Light
light_terms.overview: This chapter introduces the fundamental vocabulary of light — luminous and non-luminous objects, transparent, translucent and opaque materials, and the rectilinear propagation of light that explains how shadows form.
light_terms.deepDivePurpose: Precise terminology for light — knowing the difference between a luminous source and a reflecting object, or between transparent and translucent materials — is the essential foundation for understanding every later topic in optics, from reflection to lenses.
recap: Luminous objects produce their own light (like the Sun); non-luminous objects are only visible because they reflect light produced elsewhere (like the Moon).

A transparent material lets light pass through clearly (like glass); a translucent material lets some light through but scatters it (like frosted glass); an opaque material blocks light almost entirely.
Light travels in straight lines, a property called rectilinear propagation, which is why opaque objects cast sharp shadows.
The image formed by a plane mirror is virtual, erect, laterally inverted, and the same size as the object.
Transparency and colour are separate properties; a colourless material is not necessarily transparent.

reflection_plane.title: Reflection of Light on Plane Surfaces
reflection_plane.overview: This chapter covers the laws of reflection, the properties of images formed by plane mirrors, and how curved mirrors and devices like periscopes make use of reflection.
reflection_plane.deepDivePurpose: The laws of reflection are precise and predictable enough to power real optical instruments, from the simple periscope to complex telescopes, all built on the same underlying rule: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
recap: The First Law of Reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The Second Law of Reflection: the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane.
A plane mirror's image is virtual, erect, laterally inverted (not upside down), and exactly as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Concave mirrors converge light and can magnify (used in torches and dentist's mirrors); convex mirrors diverge light and always show a smaller, wider view (used in vehicle mirrors).
A periscope relies on two mirrors angled at exactly 45° to redirect light around obstacles to the viewer's eye.

heat_effects.title: Heat Energy and Its General Effects
heat_effects.overview: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one. This chapter covers the three general effects heat can have on a substance — a rise in temperature, expansion, and a change of state.
heat_effects.deepDivePurpose: Recognising these three general effects explains everyday observations, from why a metal lid expands and becomes easier to open under hot water, to why ice stays at 0°C for a while as it melts instead of instantly warming up.
recap: Heat energy added to a substance generally causes one or more of three effects: a rise in temperature, expansion, or a change of state.
During a change of state, added heat energy is used to break or form bonds between particles, temporarily pausing any rise in temperature.
Removing heat energy generally causes a substance to contract and its temperature to fall.
Different substances expand by different amounts for the same rise in temperature, which is why a bimetallic strip (made of two different metals) bends when heated.
A rise in temperature is calculated simply as the final temperature minus the initial temperature.

temperature_measurement.title: Temperature and Its Measurement
temperature_measurement.overview: Temperature measures how hot or cold an object is, and is measured using a thermometer calibrated against fixed reference points. This chapter covers the Celsius, Kelvin and Fahrenheit scales and how to convert between them.
temperature_measurement.deepDivePurpose: Understanding temperature scales and their conversions is essential for interpreting scientific data, weather reports and recipes from different parts of the world, all of which may use different temperature scales.
recap: A thermometer measures temperature and is typically calibrated using the ice point (0°C) and steam point (100°C) of water.
The Celsius scale is used in everyday life in most countries; the Kelvin scale, used in scientific work, starts at absolute zero and has no negative values.
To convert Celsius to Kelvin, add 273 (K = °C + 273); to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, use °F = °C × 9/5 + 32.
Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of a substance's particles, which is different from the total heat energy it contains.
A thermostat uses a temperature reading to automatically control a heating or cooling system, unlike a thermometer, which simply measures and displays temperature.

thermal_expansion.title: Thermal Expansion and Its Applications
thermal_expansion.overview: Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled, with gases expanding the most and solids the least. This chapter covers calculating expansion and the real-world applications and precautions this property requires.
thermal_expansion.deepDivePurpose: Thermal expansion, though often small in a single object, must be carefully accounted for in large structures like bridges and railway tracks, where engineers deliberately build in expansion gaps to prevent buckling and damage.
recap: Thermal expansion is the increase in a substance's size when heated; gases expand the most, followed by liquids, then solids, for the same temperature rise.
A rod's new length after expansion is its original length plus the amount it expands.
Bimetallic strips bend when heated because the two different metals in them expand at different rates.
Small gaps are deliberately left in railway tracks, bridges and window frames to allow for safe thermal expansion in hot weather.
Ignoring thermal expansion over a large structure can cause serious buckling, even though the expansion of any single small part seems negligible.

transmission_heat.title: Transmission of Heat
transmission_heat.overview: Heat travels from a hotter place to a colder one through three modes: conduction (through solids), convection (through liquids and gases), and radiation (through empty space, as electromagnetic waves). This chapter covers identifying each mode and understanding conductors and insulators.
transmission_heat.deepDivePurpose: Understanding the three modes of heat transfer explains countless everyday design choices, from insulated pan handles that block conduction, to thermos flasks that block conduction and convection, to solar panels that capture radiation.
recap: Conduction transfers heat through direct particle-to-particle contact, and is most effective in solids, especially metals.
Convection transfers heat through the bulk movement of a heated liquid or gas, as warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler, denser fluid sinks.
Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves and needs no medium at all, which is how the Sun's heat reaches Earth through space.
Metals are good conductors of heat because of their free electrons; materials like wood, rubber and trapped air are poor conductors (insulators).
Dark, matte surfaces absorb radiant heat more effectively than light-coloured or shiny surfaces, which instead reflect more of it away.

sound_production.title: Sound: Its Production and Propagation
sound_production.overview: Sound is produced by the vibration of an object and travels as a longitudinal wave through a material medium. This chapter covers how different instruments produce sound, and why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
sound_production.deepDivePurpose: Understanding that sound requires a vibrating source and a medium to travel through explains everything from why astronauts must communicate by radio in space, to why different instruments produce their distinctive sounds.
recap: Sound is produced by the vibration of an object, whether a string, a membrane, a column of air, or a solid prong.
Sound is a longitudinal wave that requires a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel, and cannot travel through a vacuum.
The classic 'bell jar' experiment, where a ringing bell fades to silence as air is pumped out, demonstrates that sound needs a medium.
Sound actually travels faster through solids than through air, since particles in a solid are packed closely together.
A vibrating source's frequency (vibrations per second) determines how many complete vibrations occur in a given time.

reflection_sound.title: Reflection and Characteristics of Sound
reflection_sound.overview: Sound can reflect off hard surfaces to produce an echo, and is described by characteristics like pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude). This chapter covers calculating echo distances and the relationship between speed, frequency and wavelength.
reflection_sound.deepDivePurpose: Understanding sound's reflection and characteristics underlies technologies like SONAR (which times echoes to locate underwater objects) and audio engineering (which precisely controls pitch and loudness independently).
recap: An echo is heard when reflected sound reaches the ear at least 0.1 seconds after the original sound, and its distance can be calculated using Distance = (Speed × Time) ÷ 2.
Pitch depends on frequency (higher frequency means higher pitch); loudness depends on amplitude (greater amplitude means louder sound) — these are independent properties.
An echo (or ultrasonic/infrasonic sound) all involve sound behaving in specific, well-defined ways beyond simple hearing.
Speed, frequency and wavelength are related by Speed = Frequency × Wavelength.
A sound wave's time period (time for one complete vibration) is the reciprocal of its frequency.

magnetism_laws.title: Laws of Magnetism and Test for a Magnet
magnetism_laws.overview: Magnets follow two consistent laws — like poles repel, unlike poles attract, and poles always exist in pairs. This chapter covers these laws, how electromagnets work, and the reliable test used to confirm whether an object is a genuine magnet.
magnetism_laws.deepDivePurpose: Knowing the true test for a magnet (repulsion, not just attraction) prevents a very common mix-up between magnets and ordinary magnetic materials, and understanding electromagnets explains devices from doorbells to industrial cranes.
recap: The First Law of Magnetism: like poles repel each other, and unlike poles attract each other.
The Second Law of Magnetism: magnetic poles always exist in pairs and can never be isolated into a single pole, even by breaking a magnet.

Attraction alone does not prove an object is a magnet, since ordinary magnetic materials (like iron) are also attracted to magnets; only repulsion of a known like pole proves an object is a genuine magnet.
An electromagnet's magnetic strength is directly proportional to the number of turns of wire in its coil, for a fixed current.
A soft iron core strengthens an electromagnet by concentrating the magnetic field produced by the current-carrying coil.

electric_circuit.title: Electric Circuit and Its Components
electric_circuit.overview: An electric circuit is a closed path through which electric current can flow, built from components like cells, switches, and fuses, connected in series or parallel. This chapter covers circuit components, series versus parallel circuits, and basic circuit calculations.
electric_circuit.deepDivePurpose: Understanding circuits and their components explains why household wiring uses parallel circuits (so one blown bulb doesn't cut power to the whole house), and forms the foundation for all electrical and electronic technology.
recap: Good electrical conductors (like copper) have free electrons that carry current easily; insulators (like rubber) do not.
A cell provides voltage, a switch opens or closes the circuit, and a fuse breaks the circuit automatically if too much current flows.
In a series circuit, components share a single current path, so one failure breaks the whole circuit; in a parallel circuit, each branch works independently.
Cells connected in series add their voltages together; V = I × R relates voltage, current and resistance in a circuit.

Adding more bulbs in series (with the same cells) makes them dimmer, since the same voltage is shared across more resistance; adding more bulbs in parallel does not dim existing bulbs, since each branch still receives the full source voltage.
